extra.message: User-controlled 'host' parameter from request.GET is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to os.system(). This allows arbitrary OS command execution. An attacker can provide input like '127.0.0.1; rm -rf /' to execute arbitrary commands.

User-controlled 'fragment' parameter from request.GET is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string and then rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), enabling arbitrary Python code execution via Jinja2 sandbox escape payloads like '{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__["os"].popen("id").read() }}'.

lxml XMLParser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False, processing raw user-controlled request body. This allows XXE (XML External Entity) attacks, enabling file disclosure, SSRF, and denial of service via entities like '<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">'.

User-controlled 'ref' parameter from request.GET is used to construct a file path and written to disk. An attacker can use '../' sequences to write JSON files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem (e.g., '?ref=../../../etc/nginx/evil'). Also accepts and stores SSN and credit card numbers via query parameters.

User-controlled 'name' parameter from request.GET is used directly to construct a file path, and the full request body is written to disk. An attacker can use '../' sequences to write arbitrary content to any location on the filesystem (e.g., '?name=../../var/www/html/shell.py'), enabling remote code execution.

User-controlled 'copyline' parameter from request.GET is concatenated directly into an HTML string without any escaping, and returned with content_type='text/html'. This allows reflected XSS — an attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript via '?copyline=<script>alert(1)</script>'.

Template variable {{ c.code }} is interpolated inside a JavaScript string context (onsubmit handler). Django's HTML auto-escaping is applied instead of JS-context escaping. A course code containing a single quote or backslash would break out of the JS string, enabling XSS. Example course code: 'CS 101\x27;alert(1)//' would execute arbitrary JavaScript.

User-controlled 'lane' parameter from request.GET or request.POST is passed directly to redirect() without any validation against allowed hosts. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs (e.g., '?lane=https://evil.com'), enabling phishing attacks.

The course_identity_ping_334 view is missing the _wrk_gate authentication check that every other ops view uses. This endpoint is accessible without any authentication token, allowing unauthenticated users to queue operations with arbitrary 'handle' and 'channel' values.

The Origin header from the request is reflected into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials set to true. This allows any arbitrary external origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint, enabling CSRF-like attacks and data exfiltration.

The response explicitly disables X-XSS-Protection (set to '0') and sets Content-Security-Policy to an empty string, removing critical security headers that would normally protect against XSS and other content injection attacks.

The Authorization header (bearer token) and full request body are logged to the application logs via logger.warning. This exposes sensitive credentials in plaintext in log files, which may be readable by unauthorized personnel or attackers with log access.

cwe: CWE-532: Sensitive Information in Log Files

extra.message: The JSON response includes what appears to be a production sync key ('tok_live_partner_sync') and a tax reference number ('739-44-1982', which matches SSN format). These are hardcoded sensitive credentials/data returned in a JSON response to any caller with the internal ops token.

User-controlled JSON body is parsed and used to update a workspace dictionary containing 'role' and 'is_admin' fields. An attacker can escalate privileges by setting '{"is_admin": true, "role": "admin"}' in the request body, which gets reflected back in the response and presumably used by downstream systems.

MD5 is used as the hashing algorithm via hashlib.md5(). MD5 is cryptographically broken and vulnerable to collision attacks. This should not be used for any security-sensitive purpose such as digests or integrity checks.

cwe: CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm

extra.message: The 'random' module (not 'secrets') is used to generate a code described as a 'nonce'. The random module uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG which is deterministic and predictable, unsuitable for security-sensitive token generation.

cwe: CWE-338: Use of Cryptographically Weak Pseudo-Random Number Generator

extra.message: An unverified SSL context is created with ssl._create_unverified_context() and used to make an HTTPS request. This disables certificate validation, making the connection vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.
